Many people never learn that their illness may be connected to the water they drank or the products they used. PFAS exposure claims are being pursued nationwide.

Overview

The "Forever Chemicals" Problem

PFAS — per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — are a family of synthetic chemicals used since the 1940s to make products resistant to heat, grease, stains and water. They are called "forever chemicals" because they do not meaningfully break down in the environment or in the human body, and instead accumulate over time.

They are also close to unavoidable. A 2023 United States Geological Survey study estimated that nearly half of the tap water in the United States may contain at least one PFAS compound. Beyond drinking water, exposure routes include AFFF firefighting foam, non-stick cookware, stain-resistant carpets and fabrics, food packaging, and some cosmetics.

A growing body of scientific research has associated long-term PFAS exposure with several serious conditions, and litigation is now proceeding against the manufacturers who made and sold these chemicals — in many cases while holding internal research about their risks.

An important point that surprises people: you do not need to have worked on a military base to have a claim. Firefighters, industrial workers, and residents of communities with contaminated municipal or well water may all be affected. If you have been diagnosed with one of the illnesses below and believe you were exposed, call 850-215-2195 for a free case evaluation.

What We Handle

Illnesses Linked to PFAS Exposure

Research has associated PFAS exposure with the conditions below. A diagnosis does not by itself establish a claim — causation has to be evaluated on your facts.

  • Kidney and testicular cancer — Among the conditions most consistently associated with PFAS exposure in published research.
  • Liver, bladder and pancreatic cancer — Cancers reported in studies of populations with elevated long-term PFAS exposure.
  • Thyroid cancer and thyroid disease — Including disruption of normal thyroid hormone function.
  • Blood cancers — Including leukemia and lymphoma reported in exposed populations.
  • Ulcerative colitis — An inflammatory bowel condition associated with PFAS exposure in research literature.
  • Preeclampsia and low birth weight — Pregnancy complications reported in studies of women with elevated PFAS levels.
Our Process

How a PFAS Claim Is Built

These cases turn on establishing exposure and connecting it to a diagnosis.

01

Establish Your Exposure

We identify how and where you were exposed — municipal or well water at a specific address, occupational contact with AFFF firefighting foam, or industrial use — and gather the records, water testing data and work history that document it.

02

Connect Exposure to Diagnosis

We collect your complete medical records and work with medical experts to evaluate whether your diagnosis fits the conditions research has associated with PFAS, and whether the timing and level of exposure support the connection.

03

Pursue the Manufacturers

Claims are brought against the chemical manufacturers and other responsible parties, often within coordinated multi-district litigation. We handle the filing, the evidentiary requirements and the negotiation.

FAQ

PFAS Contamination — Frequently Asked Questions

PFAS are a large family of manufactured chemicals used since the 1940s to make products repel water, grease, heat and stains. The carbon-fluorine bond that makes them so effective also makes them extraordinarily persistent — they do not meaningfully degrade in the environment or in the body, which is why they are commonly called "forever chemicals."

Because they accumulate, exposure that happened years ago can still be relevant today.

No. That is a common misunderstanding. Military firefighting training sites are well-known contamination sources because of AFFF foam, but they are far from the only route.

Municipal water supplies, private wells near industrial or airport sites, civilian firefighting, and certain manufacturing jobs are all potential exposure pathways. Residents of affected communities may have claims without any military connection at all.

Published research has associated PFAS exposure with kidney and testicular cancer, liver, bladder, pancreatic and thyroid cancers, blood cancers, thyroid disease, ulcerative colitis, and pregnancy complications including preeclampsia and low birth weight.

Association is not the same as proof of causation in an individual case. Whether your diagnosis supports a claim depends on your exposure history, the timing, and the medical evidence — which is what an evaluation is for.

Often you would not, which is the heart of the problem. Useful starting points are where you have lived and whether that water system has been tested for PFAS, whether you worked in firefighting, aviation, manufacturing or chemical processing, and whether you lived near a military installation, airport, industrial plant or landfill.

Part of our work is establishing exposure from water testing data, employment records and site histories — you are not expected to prove it yourself before calling.

Deadlines in these cases are complicated. They can turn on when you were diagnosed and when you reasonably should have connected the illness to an exposure, rather than simply when the exposure occurred — and different states apply different rules.

Because the analysis is genuinely fact-specific and the consequence of waiting is losing the claim entirely, do not try to work this out from a website. Call 850-215-2195 and have your dates reviewed.

Nothing. The case evaluation is free, and PFAS claims are handled on a contingency basis — you pay no attorney's fee unless compensation is recovered for you.
